stories.headline: Centre calls special Parliament sitting from November 30, with delimitation bill expected
stories.dek: The Union Cabinet is due to meet on Friday, and the government is counting on the DMK and NCP(SP) to reach the two-thirds majority a constitutional amendment needs.
stories.summary: The government has asked for Lok Sabha to reconvene on November 30 and Rajya Sabha on December 2, with the sitting ending by December 3. Congress calls it an assault on the Constitution; the NDA is seeking support to pass the women's quota bill.
body: The government has asked the Lok Sabha to reconvene on Monday, November 30, and the Rajya Sabha on Wednesday, December 2, for what it calls essential government business.

Parliamentary Affairs Minister Kiren Rijiju said on X that both Houses may conclude on December 3, depending on the business. He did not name the bills. The Union Cabinet is expected to meet on Friday and take up the delimitation-linked women's quota bill, people aware of the plans said.

The bill matters because it ties 33 per cent reservation for women in the Lok Sabha and state assemblies from the 2029 elections to a redrawing of constituencies. The Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill, 2026, would also raise the Lok Sabha's size to about 850 seats.
The bill failed in the Lok Sabha in April. The vote was 298 to 230, short of the two-thirds majority needed for a constitutional amendment. The government withdrew two linked bills afterwards.

The numbers have since shifted. Twenty Trinamool Congress MPs merged with the Nationalist Citizens Party of India and pledged support to the NDA. Six Shiv Sena (UBT) MPs joined the Shinde-led Shiv Sena, and the Shiromani Akali Dal has rejoined the alliance. That takes the NDA to about 325 in the Lok Sabha, according to Deccan Herald's count.

A two-thirds majority in the present House of 540 members would need about 360 votes. Adding the DMK's 22 MPs and the NCP (Sharadchandra Pawar)'s eight would give about 355. The NDA is also approaching smaller parties and independents, including the YSRCP, JMM, VCK and RLP. In the Rajya Sabha, the NDA has 155 members and needs 162.
The NCP (SP) has said it will examine the bill's text before deciding. No sources named a DMK position.

Congress leader Jairam Ramesh said the government was seeking a "super-tainted two-thirds majority" and asked: "Can there be a great insult to and assault on the Constitution?" Congress MP Manish Tewari said the request "mocks the institution of Parliament" and that a special sitting should not replace a regular Winter Session.

The Congress Parliamentary Strategy Group will meet on Friday at 4.30pm at Sonia Gandhi's residence to decide its approach. Opposition parties are also expected to raise the revision of electoral rolls.
keyFacts: The Monsoon Session ended on August 13 but Parliament was not prorogued, so the Houses can be reconvened at short notice.
The April 17 vote on the 131st Amendment Bill was 298 to 230 in the Lok Sabha.
The Rajya Sabha has 242 members; the NDA has 155 and needs 162 votes.
The 2023 women's reservation law remains in force, and the Opposition wants it delinked from delimitation.
stories.background: The story so far: The government introduced the 131st Constitution Amendment Bill and linked delimitation bills in April 2026 to implement women's quota from 2029. The amendment failed in the Lok Sabha on April 17, and the linked bills were withdrawn. The Opposition said the quota could be given within the current setup. Since then, MPs have moved from the Trinamool Congress and Shiv Sena (UBT) to NDA-aligned parties. The special sitting is the government's next attempt.
stories.whatNext: The Union Cabinet meets on Friday, and the Lok Sabha is due to reconvene on November 30.

stories.headline: Supreme Court orders separate red warning labels for sugar, salt and fat on packaged food
stories.dek: The court told the food regulator to base the labels on total sugar and saturated fat, not added sugar and added fat, and to redo its threshold levels.
stories.summary: The Supreme Court on Thursday directed the FSSAI to bring in front-of-pack warnings, with a separate red hexagon for high sugar, high salt and high fat. It rejected the regulator's 'added sugar' approach and a single combined label.
body: The Supreme Court on Thursday directed the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) to put separate red hexagon warnings for high sugar, salt and fat on the front of packaged foods.

The order affects makers and buyers of everyday products, from chips and biscuits to fizzy drinks. A bench of Justices JB Pardiwala and K Vinod Chandran passed it in a 131-page judgment on a petition by the non-profit 3S and Our Health Society.

The FSSAI had proposed a single red hexagon reading "High Sugar", "High Saturated Fat" and "High Salt". The court said each nutrient must get its own hexagon, with a matching pictogram and the words "High Fat", "High Sugar" or "High Salt".
Each hexagon must cover at least 4 to 5 per cent of the front panel, the court said, in line with practice abroad. The font must be "prominent, conspicuous and readily legible".

The court also rejected the regulator's plan to trigger warnings on added sugar and added fat. It directed the FSSAI to treat total sugars and saturated fat as the nutrients of concern, alongside salt.

The bench said a laboratory cannot tell added sugar from natural sugar in a finished product, so the rule could not be enforced. It said Dietary Guidelines for Indians 2024 threshold values, which were calculated on added sugar and added fat, must not be adopted as they stand.

The FSSAI must redo the thresholds on evidence. The court said thresholds set too low would put warnings on almost every product and cause "label fatigue". Thresholds set too high would let most products escape the label.

The court told the regulator to keep to its own timeline. The FSSAI had said the rules would come into force within four months of draft regulations being notified. "Every day of delay means that packaged foods continue to be sold without such labels," the court said.

Rajiv Shankar Dvivedi, lead counsel for 3S and Our Health, welcomed the ruling. The All India Consumer Products Distributors Federation called the order "a significant step" but warned against rules that disadvantage small domestic makers. It asked the FSSAI for guidance on disposing of stock and relabelling.

The court asked the FSSAI to report back on its progress by affidavit in ten weeks. Once the final rules are notified, firms will have 365 days before the labels become compulsory, and they may use them sooner.
keyFacts: The judgment runs to 131 pages and was written by Justice JB Pardiwala.
Labels become mandatory 365 days after final notification of the rules.
The FSSAI must file a progress affidavit after ten weeks.
The FSSAI floated its star-rating draft in 2022; it drew more than 14,000 comments.
The court asked the Centre to ensure strict implementation of school nutrition regulations.
stories.background: The petition by 3S and Our Health Society sought warning labels instead of the star-rating system the FSSAI floated in 2022. Earlier, the bench questioned whether the regulator was yielding to corporate pressure. On August 28 the FSSAI filed an affidavit proposing red hexagonal labels for products high in two or more of added saturated fat, added sugar and salt.
stories.whatNext: The FSSAI must file a progress affidavit in ten weeks, and labels become mandatory 365 days after final notification.

stories.headline: UP draft voter roll shows deepest deletions in seats the BJP led in 2024
stories.dek: Uttar Pradesh's chief electoral officer says the Election Commission holds no religion-wise voter data, after Chief Minister Adityanath said 1.2 crore Hindu voters were missing from the rolls.
stories.summary: An analysis of Uttar Pradesh's draft voter roll found the BJP led in 20 of the 25 assembly seats with the largest deletions since 2024. The state's chief electoral officer said the Election Commission has no data on voters' religion.
body: An analysis of Uttar Pradesh's draft voter roll released on November 17 found that the Bharatiya Janata Party led in 20 of the 25 assembly constituencies with the largest deletions of voters since the 2024 Lok Sabha election.

The finding matters for the Assembly elections due early next year. It shows where the electorate has shrunk most after a special intensive revision (SIR), the Election Commission's fresh preparation of voter lists, which ran from November 2025 to April 2026.

Scroll compared the 2024 voter lists with the new draft at the level of assembly constituencies. Allahabad North had the highest net deletion in percentage terms, at 34.4%. Lucknow Cantt, the seat of Deputy Chief Minister Brijesh Pathak, followed at 34.3%.
Most of the seats with the largest deletions are urban, in cities such as Allahabad, Lucknow, Agra and Kanpur. Of the 25, the Congress led in four and the Samajwadi Party in one.

The BJP led in 162 assembly segments in 2024, and the Samajwadi Party in 183. The state's electorate has shrunk by an average of 12%. In seats the BJP led, the average fall is 12.9%. In Samajwadi Party seats it is 10.7%. Of the 25 seats with the lowest deletions, mostly rural, the Samajwadi Party led in 13 and the BJP in 11.

The SIR removed more than 2 crore voters, about 13.4% of the electorate. In December 2025, Adityanath told a party meeting there was a gap of four crore missing voters, and said 90% of them were BJP voters. He has since alleged that 1.2 crore Hindu voters were missing from the rolls and that Muslim electors rose by 1.6%. It is not clear what data he cited.

Chief Electoral Officer Navdeep Rinwa told The Indian Express on Thursday that the Election Commission keeps no data on religion or caste. Form 6, used to apply for inclusion, has no such column, he said. He said about 2.5 crore eligible people are not on the list, but he could not say how many belong to any religion or caste.

Rinwa said he had no data to agree or disagree with the chief minister, and did not think Adityanath was questioning the Commission. On November 13, Samajwadi Party chief Akhilesh Yadav asked the Commission to say where the chief minister got his figures. He called the claim a conspiracy to create fear.

BJP figures have offered explanations. A party leader told The Indian Express that many voters had multiple ID cards and that urban voters moved to rural addresses. A functionary in Prayagraj told The Wire that many of those deleted were students who moved away. Agra Cantt MLA Giriraj Singh Dharmesh told Print that 70–80% of deletions in his seat were justified, but the rest needed examination.
Separately, Rinwa said on Wednesday that booth level officers will check flagged discrepancies in voter details. No changes will be made without the voter's consent and a signed Form 8, he said.
keyFacts: About 18.8 lakh voters were added to the draft list as of November 17, taking the electorate to 13.5 crore.
Claims and objections can be filed until December 16; applications will be cleared by December 28.
Final rolls are due on January 4.
The qualifying date for the 2027 summary revision is January 1, 2027.
stories.background: The story so far: the Election Commission ran a special intensive revision of UP's rolls from November 2025 to April 2026, removing more than 2 crore voters. In December 2025 Adityanath spoke of four crore missing voters. A special summary revision began on November 17, with a draft roll adding about 18.8 lakh names. Adityanath's claim of 1.2 crore missing Hindu voters has drawn a response from Akhilesh Yadav and the state's chief electoral officer.
stories.whatNext: Claims and objections on the draft roll close on December 16, applications are to be cleared by December 28, and final rolls are due on January 4.

stories.headline: Centre tells Delhi HC lookout circular against Saurav Das was sought by Mumbai Police
stories.dek: Mumbai Police later said it has also issued circulars against CJP leaders Abhijeet Dipke and Ashutosh Ranka over an October 2 protest at Shivaji Park that it calls unauthorised.
stories.summary: The Centre told the Delhi High Court that Mumbai Police sought the lookout circular that led to Cockroach Janta Party co-convener Saurav Das being stopped at the airport. Mumbai Police said two other party leaders face similar circulars.
body: The Centre told the Delhi High Court on Thursday that a lookout circular against Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) co-convener Saurav Das was issued at the request of Mumbai Police.

Das was stopped at Delhi airport before a flight to London this week. He had planned to speak at universities in the United Kingdom, including Oxford, on what he calls the cockroach movement. A lookout circular is a notice to immigration authorities to track, or stop, a person's travel abroad.

Additional Solicitor General Chetan Sharma, for the Centre, told Justice Amit Mahajan that the circular was issued on November 23. Another account of the hearing gave the dates as November 22 and 23. Senior advocate Akhil Sibal, for Das, said Das had not been told of any circular when he was stopped.
Sibal asked for a copy and for details of when it was issued and for which offence. Sharma said the Centre could not provide a copy and that Das could challenge the circular in separate proceedings.

Sharma also cited what he called multiple discrepancies in Das's passport, relating to place of birth, schooling, address and parentage. He said Das had left the father's name column blank. He said these could have a bearing on Das's Indian citizenship.

The Ministry of External Affairs said on Wednesday that the Regional Passport Office in Chennai issued Das a show-cause notice on November 23. It asked him to explain his place of birth within seven days and advised him not to use the passport until he replied. Sharma said the advice was in Das's favour, since an unsatisfactory reply could leave him stranded abroad.

Sibal argued that a pending reply to a show-cause notice does not allow a citizen to be stopped from travelling, which he called a fundamental right. Das has said his passport was issued in 2019 and that the notice did not set out the alleged discrepancies. He has said it reached him by email about five hours before his flight.

Later on Thursday, a senior Mumbai Police official said circulars have also been issued against CJP leaders Abhijeet Dipke and Ashutosh Ranka. He said they relate to an FIR over a protest at Shivaji Park in Dadar on Gandhi Jayanti, October 2, for which police had denied permission. The official said the circulars aim to stop the three leaving the country during the investigation.

The FIR was registered at Shivaji Park police station on October 3, and names the organisers and 400 to 500 unidentified participants. Police invoked Sections 189 and 223 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, on unlawful assembly and disobeying a public servant's order, and provisions of the Maharashtra Police Act.

Speaking at a CJP rally in Nagpur, Dipke referred to the circular against him. "Where is Abhijeet Dipke? I am here in Samvidhan Chowk. What will you do? Arrest me," he said. The High Court will hear the matter next on December 9.
keyFacts: Justice Amit Mahajan is hearing Das's petition against being stopped from travelling.
The Chennai passport office issued Das a show-cause notice on November 23, seeking a reply within seven days.
The Mumbai FIR was registered on October 3 and mentions 400 to 500 unidentified participants.
CJP members at the October 2 protest demanded the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.
stories.background: The story so far: Das, a CJP co-convener, was stopped at Delhi airport late on Monday night, November 23, before a flight to London. The Ministry of External Affairs said a show-cause notice over his place of birth had been issued that day. He moved the High Court, saying he was given no order. On Thursday the Centre disclosed the Mumbai Police circular, and police named two more CJP leaders facing similar circulars.
stories.whatNext: The Delhi High Court will hear Das's petition next on December 9.

stories.headline: Myanmar's leader says country will not follow 'inappropriate' parts of ICJ genocide ruling
stories.dek: Min Aung Hlaing did not say which orders Myanmar rejects, in his first public comments since the court found the state committed genocide against the Rohingya.
stories.summary: Myanmar's president, Min Aung Hlaing, said the country will not comply with parts of the International Court of Justice's genocide ruling that it considers inappropriate. He said the word genocide had seriously damaged Myanmar's reputation.
body: Myanmar's president, Min Aung Hlaing, has said the country will not comply with requirements of the International Court of Justice (ICJ) genocide ruling that it considers "inappropriate", state media reported on Thursday.

The ruling is final and binding, but the court cannot enforce it. The comments are the first from Min Aung Hlaing since the judgment on November 19, which ordered Myanmar to investigate and punish suspects, pay compensation and help Rohingya refugees return.

He spoke at a meeting on Wednesday. "Myanmar would take actions appropriate for a responsible country but would not comply with requirements it considered inappropriate," state media quoted him as saying. He did not say which orders he meant.

State media said he called the case brought by The Gambia a "one-sided accusation" and said the "term 'genocide' had seriously affected the country's reputation". It added that he considered himself primarily responsible for all matters in the country and would not accept actions that undermined the nation.

The ICJ found by nine votes to six that Myanmar committed genocide in its 2017 military operations in Rakhine State. It is the first time the court has held a state responsible for genocide. The court said about 10,000 Rohingya were killed and more than 700,000 fled to Bangladesh.

Besides investigations and compensation, the court ordered Myanmar to guarantee the violations will not be repeated, restore or replace lost property and protect Rohingya from discrimination. Myanmar must report back within two years on the steps it has taken, including proposed compensation.

Myanmar's foreign ministry rejected the findings on November 20. It has said the 2016–2018 operations were counter-terrorism actions against the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army, not carried out with genocidal intent.

The court has no police power of its own. Under Article 94 of the UN Charter, The Gambia may ask the UN Security Council to act if Myanmar does not follow the judgment, and the council can then choose what steps to take. More than a dozen countries have acknowledged the ruling, and the UK has announced sanctions on senior military figures.
About 1.2 million Rohingya refugees and asylum-seekers were in Bangladesh as of June 30, according to UNHCR figures.
keyFacts: The ICJ ruling was adopted by a majority of nine votes to six on November 19.
Myanmar has two years to report on the measures it has taken, including proposed compensation.
UNHCR recorded 1.2 million Rohingya refugees and asylum-seekers in Bangladesh and 22,400 in India at June 30.
Min Aung Hlaing became civilian president this year after leading the 2021 coup.
stories.background: The Gambia brought the case in 2019 under the 1948 Genocide Convention over the 2017 military operations in Rakhine State. Min Aung Hlaing commanded the military then, seized power from Aung San Suu Kyi's elected government in 2021 and became president in 2026 after restricted elections. The UK and 13 other countries acknowledged the ruling on Monday, and the UK froze assets of five military figures.
stories.whatNext: Myanmar must report to the ICJ within two years on the measures it has taken, and The Gambia can go to the UN Security Council if it does not comply.

stories.headline: Supreme Court says 'self-proclaimed' journalists may not get same protection at protests
stories.dek: The court sent seven Kerala journalists' complaints to its inquiry committee and said it would separately examine who counts as a journalist and what rights they have.
stories.summary: The Supreme Court said on Thursday that safeguards for accredited journalists covering protests may not extend to self-proclaimed ones. It will examine who qualifies as a journalist, while an inquiry committee reviews allegations of police excess in Delhi.
body: The Supreme Court on Thursday said that self-proclaimed journalists may not have the same legal protection as accredited journalists when covering protests, and agreed to examine the distinction.

The question affects reporters, freelancers and social media content creators who cover demonstrations, and the police who deal with them. The court said it would look at what rules should govern police dealings with journalists at protest sites.

A bench of Chief Justice Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana was hearing petitions by the Kerala Union of Working Journalists. The union alleges that Delhi Police detained, manhandled and forcibly removed journalists covering October protests in Delhi demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.

"Self-proclaimed journalists may not have the same protection as accredited journalists," Justice Bagchi said. He also said: "First, we have to define a journalist." He asked whether the term covered only people registered with the Press Council of India or employed by recognised news outlets, or also those reporting through social media reels.

The bench listed questions it would take up. These include whether accreditation or institutional affiliation should decide protection, whether journalists have any special privilege against law enforcement at protests, and whether forcibly removing a journalist from a protest site amounts to custody. It said press freedom must be balanced with public order.

The court disposed of the union's plea on seven journalists without expressing any opinion on the merits. It sent their complaints to the inquiry committee it appointed earlier, headed by former Supreme Court judge Justice Subhash Reddy. Justice Bagchi said the committee would establish whether the journalists were at the site, whether force was used and whether it was excessive.

The seven are Suhail Muhammed and VS Rahul of 24 News, Sajin of Asianet News, Roshni Rajan and Farsana of Reporter TV, Vishnuprasad of Mathrubhumi and Miji P Jose of Manorama News. The allegations include an attempt to snatch a photographer's camera and the assault of a woman journalist while she reported live.

Senior advocate PV Dinesh, for the petitioners, said they sought no special privileges. "We are just journalists, recognised journalists. Allow us to do our work," he told the bench. He argued that such distinctions could not be introduced retrospectively or made on the spot while removing people from a protest. Justice Bagchi replied that even a standard operating procedure would have to consider the status and character of the person claiming to be a journalist.

In an affidavit filed on November 18, Delhi Police said influencers, content creators and reel-makers are not covered by the court's earlier order exempting media personnel from movement restrictions at protest sites. It said it had never sought to obstruct the bona fide discharge of journalistic duties. It also claimed some protesters carried filming equipment and falsely described themselves as journalists.
keyFacts: The bench comprised Chief Justice Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana.
Seven journalists from Kerala outlets are named in the Kerala Union of Working Journalists' petition.
The inquiry committee is headed by former Supreme Court judge Justice Subhash Reddy.
Delhi Police's affidavit was filed on November 18.
Other petitioners include the Network of Women in Media, India, Free Speech Collective and Delhi Union of Journalists.
stories.background: The Supreme Court held a special sitting on October 11 and ordered that lawyers, journalists and other professionals should not be hindered in their work at the protests. The petitioners say Delhi Police violated that order. The court formed the inquiry committee on August 20 to examine alleged police excesses during earlier youth protests.

perspectives.label: Journalists' unions and petitioners
perspectives.summary: They say journalists were detained and removed while doing their work, and that distinctions cannot be made on the spot or applied retrospectively. They say they seek freedom to work, not special privileges.

perspectives.summary: It says it has not knowingly obstructed any journalist. It argues that influencers, content creators and reel-makers are not covered by the court's order, and that some protesters falsely claimed to be journalists.

stories.headline: Supreme Court quashes Bihar's early release of ex-MP Anand Mohan, orders surrender
stories.dek: The court declared Bihar's April 2023 prison rule change unconstitutional and said any fresh remission plea can be considered only after Mohan surrenders and the officer's widow is heard.
stories.summary: The Supreme Court on Thursday set aside the Bihar government's order releasing former MP Anand Mohan from his life term for the 1994 killing of Gopalganj DM G Krishnaiah. It directed him to surrender within a month.
body: The Supreme Court on Thursday quashed the Bihar government's order granting early release to former MP Anand Mohan and directed him to surrender within a month.

Mohan was serving a life term for instigating the mob that killed G Krishnaiah, the Gopalganj district magistrate, in 1994. The ruling returns him to prison and decides whether a state can change its jail rules in a way that frees a convict in the murder of a public servant.

A bench of Justices Dipankar Datta and Sheel Nagu declared the Bihar government's April 10, 2023 notification amending its prison rules "unconstitutional, invalid and inoperative". It also quashed the April 24, 2023 order granting Mohan premature release. If he does not surrender, the prison authority must take steps to take him into custody.

Justice Datta, reading out excerpts, said the state had failed to justify a legitimate public purpose for the selective remission and that the amended policy was manifestly arbitrary and violated Article 14, the constitutional guarantee of equality before the law. He said that granting Mohan early release in such circumstances was "indefensible and unsustainable in law".

The bench said Bihar is not barred from considering remission for Mohan again. Any such process must come only after he surrenders or is taken into custody, and only after Krishnaiah's widow, Umadevi Krishnaiah, is given a hearing. The court said Article 21, the right to life and liberty, is not a one-sided guarantee for the convict and also covers victims and their families.

Before the 2023 amendment, Bihar's prison rules barred early release of prisoners convicted of murdering a public servant on duty. Umadevi Krishnaiah challenged the change and the release in the Supreme Court. Her petition said the amendment was made with retrospective effect to benefit Mohan, and that Rule 481(1)(c) of the Bihar Prison Manual, 2012 makes convicts whose death sentence was commuted eligible for remission only after 20 years. She said Mohan had served 14 years.

Her petition also said the amendment demoralised civil servants in the state. Senior advocate Sidharth Luthra argued for her. The bench heard her, the Bihar government, Mohan and the State Sentence Remission Board before reserving its verdict on July 16, 2026.

A trial court sentenced Mohan to death on October 5, 2007. The Patna High Court commuted that to rigorous life imprisonment on December 10, 2008, and the Supreme Court upheld the commutation in July 2012. Krishnaiah, a 1985-batch IAS officer from Telangana, was beaten to death by a mob in Muzaffarpur district. Mohan, then an MLA, was convicted of instigating it.
keyFacts: Krishnaiah was 37 and posted as Gopalganj district magistrate when he was killed in December 1994.
Mohan was released from Saharsa jail in April 2023, after the Bihar government changed its prison rules.
The court said it was acting under Article 32 of the Constitution, which lets citizens approach it directly for rights.
Senior advocate Sidharth Luthra, with advocate Ritu Raj, argued for Umadevi Krishnaiah.
stories.background: Krishnaiah's vehicle tried to overtake the funeral procession of gangster Chhotan Shukla in Muzaffarpur district in 1994 when a mob beat him to death. Mohan was a leader in the procession. His death sentence was commuted to life in 2008. In April 2023, under the Nitish Kumar government, Bihar amended its prison rules and Mohan walked free.
stories.whatNext: Mohan must surrender to the competent prison authority within a month; any fresh remission process can begin only after that.

stories.headline: Supreme Court gives HDFC, ICICI and two others a week to sanction staff prosecution
stories.dek: If the lenders do not comply, their chairmen and managing directors must appear in court to explain why action should not be taken against them.
stories.summary: The Supreme Court directed HDFC Bank, ICICI Bank, Sammaan Capital and PNB Housing Finance to grant unconditional sanction to prosecute their officials within a week. Their top executives must appear in person if they fail, in the homebuyer subvention scheme cases.
body: The Supreme Court on Thursday directed HDFC Bank, ICICI Bank, Sammaan Capital and PNB Housing Finance to grant unconditional sanction within one week to prosecute their officials in alleged subvention scheme frauds involving builders and lenders.
The cases affect homebuyers who were asked to repay home loans even though builders had stopped paying the instalments. Many of those buyers had not received their flats.

A bench of Chief Justice Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana said the chairmen and managing directors would have to appear in court if the sanctions were not issued. The order said they would have to "show cause as to why appropriate action be not taken against them".

Under a subvention scheme, a bank pays the sanctioned loan amount directly to the builder. The builder is then to pay the monthly instalments until the flat is handed over. When builders default, the banks demand repayment from the buyers, despite tripartite agreements between buyer, builder and lender.

Additional Solicitor General Aishwarya Bhati, appearing for the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI), told the court the agency faced difficulty getting sanction under Section 19 of the Prevention of Corruption Act. This included cases where HDFC Bank had granted conditional sanction. The section requires the approval of the competent authority before a public servant can be prosecuted.
In its sixth supplementary status report, the CBI said investigation was complete in 25 of 55 registered cases. It has filed 22 chargesheets and submitted closure reports in three cases.
Chief Justice Kant said it was the "bounden duty" of banking authorities to grant sanction. "If they will not grant, we are warning them, the next order will be against them," he said.

The court told the CBI to complete the remaining investigations and asked the courts concerned to take up the chargesheets and frame charges quickly. The Chief Justice said the court would set timelines for completing the trials and would not allow delaying tactics.
The court ordered the CBI probe in April 2025. The matter will be heard again after seven to ten days to check whether the sanctions have been granted.
keyFacts: The CBI has registered 55 cases; investigation is complete in 25.
Twenty-two chargesheets have been filed and closure reports submitted in three cases.
HDFC Bank had granted conditional sanctions in some cases, the CBI told the court.
The Supreme Court ordered the CBI probe into the alleged builder-lender nexus in April 2025.
The case is titled Himanshu Singh vs Union of India.
stories.background: Homebuyers in subvention scheme projects found themselves facing loan recovery after developers defaulted on instalments they had agreed to pay under tripartite agreements. In April 2025 the Supreme Court ordered the CBI to investigate an alleged nexus between developers and financial institutions. The CBI has since registered 55 cases.
stories.whatNext: The court will take up the matter again after seven to ten days to check compliance with the order on prosecution sanctions.

stories.headline: Supreme Court rules PMLA authority needs a judicial member to confirm ED attachments
stories.dek: The court said single-member benches remain allowed, but only if that member comes from the field of law, and asked the Centre to consider setting up more than one authority.
stories.summary: The Supreme Court held on Thursday that the PMLA Adjudicating Authority must include a judicial member when it decides whether to confirm property attachments by the Enforcement Directorate. It also asked the Centre to consider restoring multiple such authorities.
body: The Supreme Court ruled on Thursday that the Adjudicating Authority under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act must include a judicial member when it decides whether to confirm the Enforcement Directorate's provisional attachment of property.

The ruling affects anyone whose property the ED attaches in a money laundering case. If the authority confirms an attachment, the government takes possession, and the owner can lose the use of the property until the trial ends.

The bench of Chief Justice of India Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana said the decision involves reading the law and weighing evidence. "Such dispossession may well endure until the conclusion of the trial for the offence of money laundering, depriving the person of the use of the property for a considerable period before the offence is proved," the court said.

The court said administrative and financial members have expertise in their fields, but legally sound adjudication needs judicial temperament and training. It held that a member from the field of law must be part of any bench deciding under Section 8(2) or passing an order under Section 8(3).

A single-member bench is still permitted, provided that member is a judicial member. The court upheld Sections 6(5)(b) and 6(7), which allow benches of one or two members, subject to the safeguards in its judgment. It said it had not made a two-member bench compulsory.

A judicial member is not needed to issue a show-cause notice under Section 8(1), the court said. It also extended the requirement to decisions on encumbrances and leasehold interests under Section 9, and on retention of property and records under Sections 20(4) and 21(4).

The court rejected the Centre's argument that the right of appeal to a judicial forum makes a judicial member unnecessary at the first stage. "An appellate forum may correct the errors in a decision; it cannot supply what the original forum lacked," it said. It also rejected the argument that the chairperson must be a judicial member, saying the statute does not support that.
The court directed the chairperson to issue an administrative circular so that every bench passing an order under Section 8(3) includes a judicial member.

Orders already passed by a single non-judicial member will not be set aside automatically. The court said that would serve neither justice nor quick adjudication. People aggrieved by such orders can challenge them on merits through the statutory appeals.

The court also urged the Union government to consider repealing the 2009 amendment that provided for only one authority and to return to multiple authorities, including regional ones. It did not direct this itself, because the amendment was not under challenge.
The court pointed to ED figures on the rising number of provisional attachment orders. The ED issued 321 such orders in 2023-24 and 461 in 2024-25. The number rose to 712 in 2025-26.
The court had reserved its verdict on September 15.
keyFacts: The bench was headed by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant, with Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana.
The Adjudicating Authority must complete adjudication of attachment orders within 180 days.
The ED has issued 3,639 provisional attachment orders since July 2005, according to figures it gave the court.
In July 2018 the Supreme Court had stayed a January 2018 Delhi High Court ruling on single-member benches.
stories.background: Under Section 5 of the PMLA, the ED can provisionally attach property it believes is proceeds of crime. Under Section 8, the Adjudicating Authority decides whether the property is involved in money laundering and whether to confirm the attachment. High courts in Delhi, Calcutta and Telangana had earlier declined to insist on a judicial member on every bench.

stories.headline: Supreme Court says Allahabad HC hijab ruling is not to be treated as precedent
stories.dek: The court issued notice to Uttar Pradesh on a Muslim women's organisation's appeal and tagged it with the pending Karnataka hijab appeals.
stories.summary: The Supreme Court said the Allahabad High Court's August 21 judgment, which upheld a school's hijab ban, shall not be treated as a precedent. A bench issued notice to Uttar Pradesh on November 20 and tagged the appeal with the Karnataka hijab cases.
body: The Supreme Court has ordered that the Allahabad High Court's August 21 judgment upholding a school's ban on the hijab in classrooms shall not be treated as a precedent.

The order affects a question that courts across the country may face: whether students can be barred from wearing a headscarf with their uniform. The Supreme Court has yet to settle the issue, and appeals from Karnataka are pending before it.

A bench of Justices Aravind Kumar and Vipul M Pancholi passed the order on November 20. It issued notice to the Uttar Pradesh government on an appeal by the Muslim Women's Study Circle. "Permission to file the petition is granted. Issue notice. Tag with Civil Appeal No. 7095/2022 and this judgment shall not be treated as precedent," the bench recorded.

The High Court had dismissed a petition by a Muslim student, Sukaina Rizvi. She sought permission to wear a headscarf with the prescribed uniform at Tagore Public School in Prayagraj. She said she had worn one since joining in class VI but was denied admission to class XI because it violated the dress code.

A High Court bench of Justices JJ Munir and Indrajeet Shukla held that no authoritative religious text had been placed on record to show a headscarf in a classroom is an essential religious practice under Article 25 of the Constitution. It said the Karnataka High Court's Full Bench ruling still had persuasive value, as the Supreme Court had not given a final ruling after its 2022 split verdict.

The High Court also held that the school's earlier tolerance in lower classes did not stop it from enforcing a uniform in higher classes. It said a uniform policy promotes discipline, equality and a religion-neutral atmosphere.

In its appeal, the Muslim Women's Study Circle called the judgment arbitrary and discriminatory. It argued that the ruling violates rights to equality, expression, religion, life and liberty, and protection against discrimination, and hurts Muslim women's access to education. It also said the Quran prescribes the hijab and that religious symbols of other communities, such as Sikh turbans, are treated differently.

The Supreme Court has also sought the school's response. The Karnataka appeals, which challenge a High Court order upholding that state's ban on hijabs in educational institutions, are yet to be decided by a larger bench.
keyFacts: The Supreme Court's order is dated November 20.
The appeal was tagged with Civil Appeal No. 7095/2022, part of the Karnataka hijab batch.
The Allahabad High Court judgment was delivered on August 21.
The school involved is Tagore Public School in Attarsuiya, Prayagraj.
stories.background: In 2022 a Supreme Court bench delivered a split verdict on appeals against the Karnataka High Court's ruling that upheld a hijab ban in educational institutions. The appeals await a larger bench. The Allahabad High Court relied in part on the Karnataka ruling in August.
stories.whatNext: The appeal will be heard with the pending Karnataka hijab appeals, which are yet to be decided by a larger bench; no date was given.

stories.headline: Health ministry bars fees and requires insurance in autism stem cell trials
stories.dek: Two notices issued on November 20 also set approval deadlines for researchers and say stem cell treatment for autism cannot be sold to families as ordinary care.
stories.summary: The Union health ministry has barred researchers from charging participants in autism stem cell trials and ordered institutions to insure them against harm. A second notice sets approval deadlines of 30 to 90 working days.
body: The Union health ministry has barred researchers from charging participants in autism stem cell trials and required institutions to insure them against research-related harm, under two notices issued on November 20.

The rules affect families of children with autism spectrum disorder, some of whom pay private clinics ₹3 lakh to ₹15 lakh per treatment cycle for stem cell procedures. The ministry said clinics cannot sell these procedures as regular treatment.

The notice addressed to caregivers says the hospital or site running a trial must arrange insurance before any research on people begins. The cover must pay compensation for injury, disability or death caused by the research. Compensation under the New Drugs and Clinical Trials Rules, 2019, applies equally to children given stem cells and those in comparison groups.

On costs, the notice said: "Anyone taking part in a stem cell clinical trial must not be asked to pay for any procedure during the course of the study." It said this covers the treatment being studied, tests, procedures, hospital stay and any other research-related costs.

Parents must be given full details of the study design and risks and must give voluntary written consent. Children's assent is needed where applicable. Parents can withdraw without affecting routine care. Research teams must also explain how children in each study group will be monitored and what happens after the trial ends.

The ministry cautioned that joining a randomised trial does not guarantee a child will receive stem cells or benefit. It advised families: "Do not stop or delay your child's existing care or developmental support in favour of an unproven intervention." It also said using a child's own cells does not make an unproven treatment safe or permissible.

The second notice sets a two-tier approval process. Cells with only basic laboratory processing need clearance from an institutional scientific panel and an ethics committee that includes outside stem cell specialists. They then go to the National Stem Cell Research Regulation Committee under the Department of Health Research, which must decide within 90 working days.

Heavily altered or engineered cells are regulated as a new drug. Researchers must apply to the Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation, which must decide within 30 working days for therapies developed in India and 90 working days for foreign ones. Site ethics committees must notify the regulator within 15 working days. All trials must be registered on the Clinical Trials Registry of India before enrolment.

Dr Anshul Dhillon, a consultant paediatric neurologist at Kailash Hospital in Noida, said stem cell therapy for autism remains investigational and should be used only within approved trials. The ministry spokesperson did not respond to queries.
The ministry has invited public feedback by email on participation in a proposed randomised controlled trial for autism. The notice does not give a closing date.
keyFacts: Both notices were issued on November 20.
Heavily altered cells are regulated as a new drug by the Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation.
The drug regulator has 30 working days for Indian therapies and 90 for foreign ones.
Trials must be registered on the Clinical Trials Registry of India before enrolment.
India has an estimated 18 million people with autism, including about 2 million children.
stories.background: A September 17 health ministry advisory warned doctors and clinics of disciplinary action and penalties for offering unproven stem cell procedures as routine care. It followed a Supreme Court judgment that patients have no right to demand experimental stem cell treatment outside regulated clinical trials.

stories.headline: Two Italian technicians die after drone strike on 'vital site' in Kuwait
stories.dek: Italy and Kuwait blame Iran for the attack on the Thursday; Tehran denies involvement, calls the incident 'suspicious' and offers to help investigate.
stories.summary: Two Italian technicians working for Rheinmetall Italia died after drones hit a site in Kuwait on Thursday. Italy and Kuwait blamed Iran, which denied responsibility and said the incident looked like a 'precooked recipe for war'.
body: Two Italian technicians working for Rheinmetall Italia died on Thursday after Iranian drones were launched at a "vital site" in Kuwait, Italy's Foreign Ministry and Kuwaiti officials said.

The deaths matter beyond the Gulf because Italy, a European Union member, is now directly affected by a war that began in February. European leaders have called for more pressure on Tehran, and talks to end the war have stalled.

The Italian ministry said an explosion caused by a drone attack occurred at a site where the two men were working. They were doing maintenance on detection antennas for the Skyguard air-defence system, the Italian news agency ANSA reported. ANSA named them as Antonio Saccoccio, 65, of Formia, and Emanuele Lo Russo, 36, of Rome.

Kuwait's Defence Ministry called it a "criminal attack". Its spokesman, Staff Colonel Saud Abdulaziz Al-Atwan, said the armed forces detected several hostile drones in Kuwaiti airspace and "dealt with them". A Kuwaiti and a Pakistani national were also hurt and taken to hospital. The ministry did not give the site's location.
Kuwaiti authorities said the Italians died from falling debris as the drones were being intercepted. Initial Kuwaiti statements had listed four wounded, including two Italians.

Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said she learned of the deaths during a European Council meeting. She posted on X that she extended "heartfelt condolences" to the families. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the EU must "step up pressure on Iran to put an end to these unacceptable attacks".

Iran denied attacking Kuwaiti airspace. Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said he had spoken to his Italian and Kuwaiti counterparts and offered condolences. "The incident is suspicious and looks like a precooked recipe for war," he wrote, adding that Iran was ready to help find the cause.

Iran's embassy in Rome warned against "false flag" operations, meaning attacks staged to blame another party, that it said aimed to widen the conflict and draw Europe in. Mohammad Marandi, a former adviser to Iran's nuclear negotiating team, said on X that Ukraine was likely behind the attack. No evidence for that claim was given in the material available, and Ukraine's response was not reported.
Ukraine has sent drone specialists to several Gulf states, including Kuwait, to help defend against Iranian drones, according to earlier announcements by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
keyFacts: The victims were aged 36 and 65 and worked for Rheinmetall Italia.
They were maintaining antennas for the Skyguard air-defence system.
A Kuwaiti and a Pakistani national were also injured.
Araghchi spoke by phone with his Italian and Kuwaiti counterparts.
Kuwait has been hit repeatedly since the war began in February.
stories.background: The story so far: The United States and Israel launched military operations against Iran in February. Iran responded with retaliatory attacks across the Gulf, including on Kuwait, a US ally that hosts American military facilities. Kuwait has repeatedly condemned the strikes. Talks to end the war have stalled. On Thursday, two Italian technicians died after drones were fired at a Kuwaiti site. Iran rejects responsibility.

stories.headline: Indian trade body urges 25% retaliatory tariffs on US goods, warns of 500,000 job losses
stories.dek: The US Trade Representative has proposed duties of up to 25% on Indian goods, falling to 17% if a trade deal is reached; India's government denies the excess-capacity charge.
stories.summary: The Chamber of Trade and Industry has asked the Indian government to match proposed US tariffs of up to 25%, saying 500,000 jobs and over US$48 billion of exports are at risk. India's commerce ministry says it is examining the US proposal.
body: An Indian trade body has urged New Delhi to impose retaliatory tariffs of 25 per cent on American goods, saying the US proposal could put 500,000 jobs at risk.
The US is India's largest export market, accounting for more than $87 billion of merchandise shipments in FY26, about a fifth of the total. The proposed duties have not taken effect.

Brijesh Goyal, chairman of the Delhi-based Chamber of Trade and Industry, said in a statement on Thursday that more than US$48 billion of Indian exports could be affected. He named textiles, leather, gems and jewellery, auto components and seafood as the sectors most exposed. The chamber has written to Prime Minister Narendra Modi asking for matching tariffs on US minerals, machinery, aircraft equipment, electronics, plastics, chemicals, and iron and steel. "India should reduce its dependence on America for all these things and look for options in other countries," Goyal said.

The US Trade Representative (USTR) proposed on Wednesday additional duties of up to 25 per cent on Indian goods and those of 13 other economies. The proposal follows investigations under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 into alleged structural excess capacity, meaning an economy making more than its market needs. The rate could fall to 17 per cent if India concludes a reciprocal trade agreement with the US. Smartphones, pharmaceuticals, semiconductors, metals, vehicles and aircraft parts are exempt, though existing duties may still apply.

India's commerce ministry said it was examining the notice. It repeated that India has no structural excess capacity in any sector and said trade concerns should be handled in the continuing talks on a Bilateral Trade Agreement.

Exporters are divided on how the rates compare with rivals. Pankaj Chadha, chairman of the Engineering Export Promotion Council, said 17 per cent may give little edge, as Bangladesh, Indonesia, Malaysia and Thailand face proposed deal rates of around 18 per cent. Vietnam and China face 20 per cent. "Our view is that as long as India and its competing countries are facing the same tariff rates, there are no issues," he said.

Atman Trivedi of the Albright Stonebridge Group, a Washington consultancy, told CNBC that India has a better bargain than its main competitors. Another analyst, Ronak Desai of the Hoover Institution, said the Modi government would be sensitive to any sense of conceding under American pressure.

Chandrima Chatterjee, secretary general of the Confederation of Indian Textile Industry, said frequent tariff changes create uncertainty over pricing and orders. Ajay Srivastava of the Global Trade Research Initiative called the proposal "a deliberate bait to extract one-sided concessions" and urged India to reject such a deal. SC Ralhan, president of the Federation of Indian Export Organisations, said there was no panic among exporters.

Data cited by the USTR show manufacturing made up an average of 13.5 per cent of India's GDP from 2021 to 2025, against a global average of 15.4 per cent. The Reserve Bank of India's capacity utilisation rate was 76.2 per cent in the April-June quarter of 2026-27.
The USTR is taking public comments until January 5, 2027. Hearings are due to begin on January 25.
keyFacts: Indian merchandise exports rose 45.06% to $49.47 billion in October; exports to the US rose 39%.
Existing Section 301 duty of 10% on Indian goods has applied since July 24, 2026.
India was flagged for possible excess capacity in seven sectors, including solar modules, steel and textiles.
India's trade surplus with the US was $57.3 billion in 2025, up from $45.2 billion in 2024.
stories.background: The US imposed a 10 per cent Section 301 duty on Indian goods from July 24, 2026, after a separate probe on forced labour. In February, President Donald Trump announced a deal with India that he said cut tariffs to 18 per cent from 50 per cent, but the trade agreement remains unsigned. On Wednesday the USTR proposed new duties of up to 25 per cent after its excess-capacity investigation. Modi and Trump are likely to meet at the G20 in Florida in December.
stories.whatNext: The USTR is accepting public comments until January 5, 2027, with hearings due to begin on January 25.

stories.headline: Samajwadi Party manifesto promises ₹5,000 monthly allowance and 25 lakh jobs in UP
stories.dek: UP BJP president Pankaj Chaudhary dismissed the document as a "dhakosla patra", while seat-sharing talks between the SP and Congress continue.
stories.summary: The Samajwadi Party released its manifesto for the 2027 Uttar Pradesh election on Thursday, promising a ₹5,000 monthly allowance for new graduates and 25 lakh state government jobs. The BJP called it a "dhakosla patra", a deceptive document.
body: The Samajwadi Party (SP) on Thursday released its manifesto for the Uttar Pradesh Assembly election, promising a monthly allowance of ₹5,000 to new graduates until they find work and 25 lakh state government jobs over five years.
The promises cover jobs, farm incomes, household costs and policing in a state where the election is expected early next year. The manifesto is titled "PDA Ka Prannpatra".

Party president Akhilesh Yadav said an SP government would give an annual cash transfer of ₹40,000 to women, senior citizens and "persons in need" from families below the poverty line. It also promised up to 300 units of free domestic electricity.

For farmers, the party promised an immediate loan waiver and a legal guarantee of minimum support prices for 23 crops and milk. The minimum support price is the rate at which the government buys a crop if market prices fall below it.

Other promises include a 50% quota in government contracts worth up to ₹5 crore for vendors from backward classes, Dalit and religious minority communities. Yadav said a caste census would be held by 2028, about 26,000 primary schools would reopen, and the laptop scheme for Class 12 students would resume.

On law and order, the party promised zero tolerance for crime, mafias and riots. It proposed a special task force against land-grabbing, cyber units in every district, and CCTV and drone surveillance in towns and villages within a year. It also promised to fill all police vacancies immediately, with 33 per cent for women.

At the launch, Yadav said the "Acche Din" the BJP promised never arrived, and that "Bure Din" would soon end. He argued that the BJP's tone had changed because it senses it will lose power. The party will release two more manifestos during the campaign, on women and on technology.

UP BJP president Pankaj Chaudhary told ANI the people of the state would not fall into the SP's "electoral trap". He called the manifesto an "unrealistic sham document" and said that when in power the SP had "only filled their own coffers". He also mocked its zero-tolerance pledge on crime, citing a "One District, One Mafia" policy during its rule. The SP has not been quoted responding to the charge.

Congress MP Imran Masood said on Thursday that an alliance does not work if one partner announces candidates while talks are on. The SP had named five candidates a day earlier. "Are we alliance partners or your servants?" he asked. He declined to comment on the manifesto.
Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge, speaking in Lucknow, attacked the BJP over inflation and unemployment. Seat-sharing talks between the two parties are still under way.
keyFacts: The SP also promised a legal guarantee of minimum support prices for 23 crops and milk.
Chandrashekhar Azad and Asaduddin Owaisi's Samajik Parivartan Morcha says it will contest all 403 seats.
The SP named five candidates on Wednesday while seat talks with Congress were still on.
Masood said Congress contested 107 seats when Yadav was chief minister.
stories.background: The story so far: The SP lost power in Uttar Pradesh in 2017 to the BJP-led National Democratic Alliance and lost again in 2022. Akhilesh Yadav was chief minister from 2012 to 2017. The BJP-led NDA won 36 of the state's 80 Lok Sabha seats in 2024. The SP is expected to fight the 2027 election with INDIA bloc partners, mainly the Congress. This week it named five candidates while seat talks continued, drawing objections from a Congress MP. On Thursday it released its manifesto.
stories.whatNext: The SP says it will release two more manifestos during the campaign, one for women and one on technology.

stories.headline: Nepal begins process to declare 213 missing Indians dead after August floods
stories.dek: The Indian Embassy in Kathmandu has asked families to raise any objections to the list of names before December 2.
stories.summary: Nepal's disaster authority has published a list of 213 missing Indian nationals as it starts the legal process to presume them dead after the August flash floods. Families have until December 2 to ask for changes through the Indian Embassy.
body: Nepal has started the legal steps to presume 213 Indian nationals dead, all missing since the August flash floods, the Indian Embassy in Nepal announced on Wednesday.
The step matters to families in India who have had no word of relatives for three months. A formal declaration of death is needed before death certificates can be issued.
The National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA) has put the list of 213 names on its website. It has invited objections, including requests to add, remove or correct details.
Family members with concerns can contact the embassy before December 2, the embassy said. It gave an email address, eoikathmandufloodsupport@gmail.com, and a mobile number, +9779851316807.

When the comment period closes, Nepal's government will settle the final list and issue the declaration of death, the embassy said. The embassy will then begin collecting death certificates from local authorities in Nepal.
The embassy said it may ask families for more details and documents along the way. It promised an update in the coming days.

The flood struck the Trishuli-Bhote Koshi river system. The NDRRMA says it killed at least 1,453 people and left more than 5,000 missing. The Bhotekoshi River carried the water downstream, sweeping away homes, vehicles, roads and bridges and damaging hydropower projects.

Nepal has also begun a wider process to declare thousands of missing people dead, authorities said on Thursday. Ram Bahadur KC said: "We have started the process to declare the missing dead by verifying their details." Figures differ between accounts: one gives more than 1,400 dead and over 5,500 missing in Nepal.
keyFacts: The embassy's press release was issued on Wednesday, November 25.
The NDRRMA published the list of 213 Indian nationals on its website.
Objections and corrections must reach the Indian Embassy before December 2.
The NDRRMA says at least 1,453 people died and more than 5,000 are missing.
An ice-rock avalanche near the Nepal-Tibet border triggered the floods, according to one account.
stories.background: Flash floods hit northern and central Nepal in August, after an ice and rock collapse near the Nepal-China border sent water and debris down the Trishuli-Bhote Koshi river system. Accounts differ on the date, giving August 23 and August 26. The NDRRMA is Nepal's disaster management body. Declaring missing people dead lets families obtain death certificates.
stories.whatNext: The comment period on the list ends on December 2, after which Nepal will finalise it and issue the declaration of death.

stories.headline: I&B ministry asks Netflix to keep Pakistani content off Indian screens ahead of Fawad Khan series
stories.dek: Two film workers' bodies have written to Prime Minister Narendra Modi seeking a ban on the show, which Netflix has scheduled for December 4.
stories.summary: The information and broadcasting ministry has asked Netflix to follow its May 2025 advisory against streaming Pakistani-origin content in India, official sources said. Film bodies AICWA and FWICE have sought a ban on the series 'Jo Bachay Hain Sang Samait Lo'.
body: The information and broadcasting ministry has asked Netflix to ensure that content originating in Pakistan is not streamed in India, official sources said on Thursday, ahead of the December 4 release of the series 'Jo Bachay Hain Sang Samait Lo'.

The ministry said it had received several complaints and representations about the possible Indian release of the show, which stars Fawad Khan, Mahira Khan and Hania Aamir. It matters to Indian subscribers because it points to what Netflix may or may not offer them on that date.

Sources said the ministry asked Netflix to adhere to an advisory dated May 8, 2025. That advisory, issued after the April 22, 2025 Pahalgam attack, asked OTT platforms and streaming services to stop offering Pakistani-origin films, web series, songs and podcasts. It cited national security and public order.

The ministry also asked Netflix to stand by a commitment it gave in June 2025. Netflix had then told the government that it had made no film or series originating in Pakistan available to subscribers in India.
Netflix has not said whether the December 4 release includes India or is aimed only at Pakistan and other countries. The trailer was released on Tuesday.

The All Indian Cine Workers Association (AICWA) wrote to Modi on November 24, seeking a ban. Its letter, signed by president Suresh Shyamlal Gupta, called Pakistan a "terrorist country" and said the release would go against the spirit of the advisory and the sentiments of the nation.

The Federation of Western India Cine Employees (FWICE), an umbrella body of 32 associations with five lakh members, also wrote to the Prime Minister. It asked him to direct the ministry and other authorities to examine the release urgently. It warned it would "ensure the shoot of all the Netflix projects comes to a halt" if the series is released in India.

FWICE president B N Tiwari told PTI: "For us, the country comes first, and Pakistani artists are not welcome." The federation has also told its members not to work with Pakistani artists and technicians.
In Pakistan, Planning and Development Minister Ahsan Iqbal criticised the demand on X. "First weaponising sports, then water, and now art and culture," he wrote, adding: "India, grow up."
The series is created, directed and produced by Momina Duraid. It adapts Farhat Ishtiaq's 2013 Urdu novel of the same name and is titled "All the Love Our Hearts Carry" in international markets.
keyFacts: The ministry's advisory is dated May 8, 2025, during Operation Sindoor.
Netflix told the ministry in June 2025 it had no Pakistani-origin film or series available in India.

stories.background: The Pahalgam attack on April 22, 2025 killed 25 Indians and one Nepali tourist. India carried out strikes on May 7, 2025, and the ministry's advisory to streaming platforms followed on May 8. The Centre also moved to block social media accounts of Pakistani officials, actors and influencers, and some YouTube channels.
stories.whatNext: The series is scheduled to premiere on Netflix on December 4.

stories.headline: Congo's confirmed Ebola cases pass 12,000 as fighting disrupts response
stories.dek: Government data show 5,904 deaths from the Bundibugyo virus outbreak, for which no vaccine or treatment is approved, as rebels and the army fight near Bunia.
stories.summary: Confirmed Ebola cases in Democratic Republic of Congo reached 12,021 on Thursday, with 5,904 deaths, government data showed. Fighting between the army and rebels is disrupting the response in Ituri province, and some responders have been evacuated.
body: Confirmed Ebola cases in Democratic Republic of Congo have passed 12,000, with 12,021 infections and 5,904 deaths, data from the country's Ministry of Health showed on Thursday.

The outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo virus, a rare species of Ebola for which no vaccine or treatment is approved. It has spread to 8 of Congo's 26 provinces since it was declared in mid-May in Ituri province, in the north-east.

Fighting between the army and Convention pour la révolution populaire (CRP) rebels resumed on Thursday morning in Iga-Barrière, a mining town about 25 kilometres north of Bunia. It sent new groups of displaced people towards the city. Bunia, the capital of Ituri, is a major hub for the Ebola response.

Dr Catherine Smallwood, the World Health Organization's Ebola incident manager, said on Wednesday that earlier fighting had stopped teams from reaching some communities. It also disrupted the monitoring of people exposed to the virus and left some treatment centres with fewer staff.

Smallwood said about a dozen people, including two WHO staff and Congolese health officials, were evacuated to Bunia on Tuesday. They had spent three days trapped in a hospital in Akwe, north-east of Bunia, during heavy crossfire.

Response teams also face poor roads and violence from residents driven by mistrust and misinformation. Ebola spreads through contact with the blood or other body fluids of people who are sick or have died. Containing it means isolating patients, tracing and monitoring contacts, and burying the dead safely.

The outbreak is not under control. Data presented by Africa CDC earlier this month showed only 15% of new cases came from contacts already known to health authorities, meaning many chains of transmission are being missed. A Reuters analysis of satellite imagery found the official death toll may be largely underestimated in two of the hardest-hit areas.
Separately, the New York Times reported that Dr Jean Kaseya, director general of Africa CDC, faces scrutiny over reports of staff intimidation and mismanagement of funds.
keyFacts: Confirmed cases stand at 12,021, with 5,904 deaths, per Congo's Ministry of Health.
The outbreak was declared in mid-May in Ituri province.
Eight of Congo's 26 provinces have reported cases.
The 2014-2016 West African outbreak infected more than 28,600 people and killed more than 11,000.
CRP was founded last year by former warlord Thomas Lubanga.
stories.background: Ebola is a viral disease with a high death rate. The 2014-2016 West African outbreak is the largest on record. Africa CDC is the African Union's public health agency, based in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia. Eastern Congo has more than 100 armed groups, and conflict there has created one of the world's most severe humanitarian crises.

stories.headline: Tata Trusts file suits in Bombay High Court against Chandrasekaran's reappointment
stories.dek: Two trusts say the September 17 Tata Sons board vote was invalid because it lacked the backing Article 121 requires, and seek ₹65 crore in damages.
stories.summary: Trustees of the Sir Dorabji Tata Trust and the Sir Ratan Tata Trust have sued in the Bombay High Court over N Chandrasekaran's reappointment as Tata Sons executive chairman. They say the September 17 resolution breached the company's Articles of Association.
body: Trustees of the Sir Dorabji Tata Trust (SDTT) and the Sir Ratan Tata Trust have filed suits in the Bombay High Court challenging the reappointment of N Chandrasekaran as executive chairman of Tata Sons for a further five years.
The Tata Trusts hold about 66 per cent of Tata Sons, the holding company of the Tata Group. The outcome could decide who leads the group after Chandrasekaran's current term ends on February 20, 2027.

The board resolution of September 17 was passed 4:1. Directors Venu Srinivasan, Harish Manwani, Anita M George and Saurabh Agrawal voted in favour. Noel Tata, chairman of Tata Trusts, voted against. Chandrasekaran recused himself as an interested director.
The suits say Manwani, acting as chair for that agenda item, used a casting vote to treat the resolution as passed. A casting vote is an extra vote used to break a tie.

The trusts argue that Article 121 of the Articles of Association requires the affirmative vote of a majority of the directors nominated by the Trusts who are present. Two such directors sit on the board, Noel Tata and Srinivasan. They split on the resolution.
The trusts say a casting vote applies only when the whole board is tied. They say it cannot replace the approval of the trust-nominated directors.

They seek a declaration that the resolution is void and an order stopping the defendants from acting on it. They also want Chandrasekaran, Manwani or any acting chair barred from using a casting vote over the trust directors' votes.

The trusts seek ₹65 crore in damages with 18 per cent annual interest. SDTT seeks ₹50 crore and the other trust ₹15 crore. The defendants are Tata Sons, Chandrasekaran, Agrawal, Manwani, George and Srinivasan. Noel Tata is also named, but no relief is sought against him.

The trusts voted on Wednesday night to authorise the suits, citing a lack of satisfactory replies to their communications since September 17. In a statement on September 20, they said the resolution had "no legal effect".
The immediate relief sought concerns the board meeting on November 30. Its agenda includes confirming the September 17 minutes and convening an extraordinary general meeting.
keyFacts: Chandrasekaran's current term as Tata Sons chairman ends on February 20, 2027.
The proposed new term runs from February 21, 2027 to February 20, 2032.
Chandrasekaran emailed the board on August 12 saying he would not seek reappointment.
The suits cite Section 10(1) of the Companies Act, 2013.
Tata Trusts hold about 66 per cent of Tata Sons.
stories.background: Chandrasekaran told the Tata Sons board on August 12 that he would not seek another term. SDTT and five other trusts passed resolutions on August 13 respecting that and asked for a selection committee under Article 118. At the September 17 meeting, he said he had reconsidered. The board then passed the resolution on a 4:1 vote. The trusts said on September 20 that it was not validly passed.
stories.whatNext: The Tata Sons board is due to meet on November 30, and the trusts want interim relief from the High Court before then.

stories.headline: Norse Atlantic suspends all flights, says it will file for bankruptcy without urgent funding
stories.dek: The low-cost long-haul airline said its board intends to seek bankruptcy if no short-term financing is found, a day after its shares fell 85%.
stories.summary: Norwegian carrier Norse Atlantic Airways suspended all flights on Thursday and said it will file for bankruptcy if it cannot secure short-term financing urgently. Its Oslo-listed shares closed 85% lower the day before, after it called its finances critical.
body: Norse Atlantic Airways suspended all its flights on Thursday and said its board intends to file for bankruptcy if short-term financing is not secured urgently.

The Norwegian low-cost carrier flies long-haul routes, including from London Gatwick. Passengers have been stranded or forced to rebook. It also affects Pakistan International Airlines (PIA), which leased Norse aircraft and crews.

In a statement to the Oslo stock exchange, Norse said its board was still considering options for short-term financing. It said it was also in talks with investors about a possible takeover that would include a financing solution. "There can be no assurance that a viable solution will be found," the airline said.
On Wednesday, Norse said its financial position was critical. Its shares closed 85% lower that day.

The first signs of trouble came on Wednesday, when PIA cancelled flights from London to Islamabad and from Manchester to Lahore because of what it called an unexpected operational suspension. The two airlines had signed a wet-lease deal in early October. Under such a deal, one airline supplies the aircraft and crew to another. PIA said it would fly its UK services with its own aircraft from Thursday.

Norse's London Gatwick to Orlando flight was also shown as cancelled. UK routes affected include Gatwick to Bangkok and Cape Town. A winter service from Manchester to Thailand was due to begin next month. CNBC found the airline was still selling tickets for flights from Friday as of 9 a.m. Oslo time on Thursday.

Two passengers told the BBC they had struggled to reach the airline. One said he rebooked on another carrier at an extra cost of £1,000. Another, stuck in South Africa, said she faced an expensive flight home. Norse said it sincerely apologised to passengers for the inconvenience.

The airline has been hit by higher jet fuel prices since the US-Israel war on Iran began in February. Unlike many European rivals, Norse does not buy fuel in advance at fixed prices, so it was fully exposed when prices rose. Its first-half loss was $94.6m.

Norse had been seeking a buyer since July. It cut about 75 jobs in May as part of a plan to save $50 million. Founder and chief executive Bjorn Tore Larsen left the airline, and Eivind Roald took over in November last year.
Cirium, an aviation analytics firm, counted 4,822 scheduled Norse flights in 2024 and 2,565 in 2026. The airline had 122 flights scheduled for November.

Indian carrier IndiGo leased six Norse 787-9 aircraft from early 2025 to launch flights to Europe and Britain. That deal ended at the end of October, with IndiGo citing airspace constraints, high fuel costs and currency pressures.

Fuel prices rose sharply after the war on Iran began in February. US low-cost carrier Spirit Airlines failed in May after being similarly exposed to fuel prices.

stories.headline: EU leaders end Brussels summit without budget deal or agreement on Ukraine loan
stories.dek: Leaders plan to try again on December 17 and 18, as Germany presses all 27 states to back a €45 billion loan for Ukraine.
stories.summary: EU leaders ended a Brussels summit on Thursday night without agreeing a 2028-2034 budget or a €45 billion loan for Ukraine, and cut short a planned second day. They will try again at a summit on December 17 and 18.
body: European Union leaders ended a summit in Brussels on Thursday night without a deal on the 2028-2034 budget, and cut short a second day of talks that had been planned for Friday.

The budget sets how the bloc spends money over seven years. It needs the approval of all 27 member states. Leaders want a deal by the end of the year because elections in France, Italy, Poland, Greece, Estonia, Finland and Slovakia next year could make talks harder.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said the day had brought "new movement" towards a smaller budget, as Germany and other net contributors, which pay in more than they receive, have demanded. He said leaders would try to settle it at a two-day summit starting December 17. European Council President Antonio Costa is expected to bring a new proposal before then.

Costa's latest proposal, presented last Saturday, puts the budget at €1.582 trillion, including €140 billion to repay pandemic-era borrowing. About €740 billion would go to farmers and poorer regions. It includes up to €100 billion for Ukraine.

Separately, the Commission has proposed a €45 billion loan to Ukraine for 2027: €25 billion for military needs and €20 billion for civilian needs. It would be repaid only when Russia pays war reparations. Costa said 24 of 27 members supported it.

Slovakia, Hungary and the Czech Republic want to stay out. Bulgaria, which had objected, said it would join the civilian part. Prime Minister Rumen Radev said: "no money from Bulgaria for weapons." Merz has said Germany will approve the budget only if all countries back the loan. "The European Union comprises of 27 Member States, not 23 or 24," he said. Slovakia's prime minister, Robert Fico, has accused Merz of blackmail. Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babiš said Ukraine financing should be negotiated separately.

Positions on the budget itself remain far apart. Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said before the summit: "We're light-years away from a solution." Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar said the chance of a deal on Thursday was "virtually zero". Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten said there was no progress yet and that talks would be more intense in December.

French politics also shaped the talks. Marine Le Pen, the far-right National Rally leader who is leading in polls for the presidential election next spring, has said France would stop financial support for Ukraine and cut its EU contributions if she won. She described the push for a deal before the vote as an attempt to deter her from defending French interests.

President Emmanuel Macron replied that Le Pen was campaigning and that it took "a peculiar kind of arrogance" to think she was already in charge. He said that if there is no deal by December 31, talks would resume in the second half of 2027, when his successor would be in office.
keyFacts: Costa's budget proposal totals €1.582 trillion for 2028-2034, including €140 billion to repay pandemic-era borrowing.
Non-EU countries such as Britain, Norway, Japan and Canada are expected to give Ukraine another €25 billion in 2027.
Greek PM Kyriakos Mitsotakis said a deal in the first half of 2027 would be practically impossible.
Germany wants future Ukraine funding decisions taken by majority vote rather than unanimity.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said considerable work remains before a deal.
stories.background: The EU long-term budget needs unanimous backing. Net contributors such as Germany, the Netherlands and Sweden want cuts and more spending on defence and competitiveness. Many southern, central and eastern states want to protect farm and regional funds. Nearly a year ago, EU leaders agreed a loan to cover most of Ukraine's government needs for two years; the Czech Republic, Hungary and Slovakia opted out of backing it.
stories.whatNext: EU leaders will try to agree the budget and the Ukraine loan at a two-day summit starting on December 17.
